displacement_rubric.high: A source ties a large loss of existing residents or businesses to the revival: a double-digit fall in the long-standing population share, or many households or long-standing businesses forced out. This holds whether or not protections came later.
displacement_rubric.moderate: Sources show rising rents or prices, a smaller loss or the loss of one group, or a loss they do not tie to the revival.
displacement_rubric.low: Sources describe protections that worked (affordability covenants, rent pacts, local or tenant ownership, buying only shop units) and no documented loss.
displacement_rubric.unknown: No source addresses displacement. Unknown does not mean none.

buildings.name: SNF Parkway Theatre

buildings.name: Uptown Theater
buildings.orig_use: Art Deco movie and stage theatre, a major venue for Black performers and civil-rights shows.

districts.lead: Semaest, a city-controlled mixed-economy company owned mainly by the City of Paris and a public bank.

milestones.event: Quad Communities Development Corporation formed; it first called for redeveloping 47th & Cottage Grove.
Urban Juncture's founder buys an abandoned liquor store at 51st & Prairie, later the Bronzeville Incubator (home of an Illinois SBDC); the Foundation buys the 1897 Forum on 43rd St in 2011.

Bronzeville Retail Initiative created (Bronzeville Alliance 2008); its 2011 task force recommends focusing retail on 47th St, a new 3rd Ward SSA, land assembly of city-owned lots and flexible zoning; 12 TIFs generate over $50M.
Shops and Lofts at 47 opens at 47th & Cottage Grove: 96 units (44 affordable, 28 public housing, 24 market), 55,000 sq ft retail anchored by Walmart Neighborhood Market, $45.6M with nearly $13M TIF.
Boxville shipping-container market opens at 51st & Calumet beside the Green Line (four containers, $500/month for half a container); 64 local enterprises in its first season.

The Forum wins a $1M Mellon grant toward a $20M restoration after a residential-to-commercial rezoning; Bronzeville Winery opens in the publicly funded 84-unit 4400 Grove (two-thirds below-market) on the Invest South/West Cottage Grove corridor.

status_now.text: In October 2026 the Bronzeville Legacy Collective (founded 2023) announced a nine-site cultural zone with $75M raised toward a $250M goal; The Forum (318-328 E 43rd St) is under construction for Q4 2029, Bronzeville Cookin' food hub at 300-314 E 51st St for Q4 2029, and the South Side Community Art Center reopening Q1 2027. The 1.5-mile Bronzeville Trail has a $5M city framework plan (2024) but an $83M+ cost and construction around 2032.

districts.lesson: A mission owner bought cheap buildings early and tested tenants in $500-a-month containers while anchor projects took a decade. The city held about 90% of the vacant land, which Waverly does not have.

milestones.event: Mt. Airy CDC founded (as Mt. Airy Village Development Corp., later Mt. Airy USA); early work acquires and rehabs neglected Germantown Ave storefronts for local merchants to own and run.
Germantown United CDC incorporated after the Germantown Settlement's assets were liquidated in bankruptcy; PIDC lists the Town Hall (vacant since 1998) for sale.
City Planning Commission adopts the Central Germantown Business District plan: 275 ground-floor spaces, 78.5% occupied, 25 projects, Storefront Improvement Program (50% up to $8,000/$12,000).

PRA buys the 49,000 sq ft YWCA at sheriff's auction; city pledges $2.2M for Maplewood Mall; Mt. Airy USA rehabs 6513 Germantown Ave and three other avenue buildings ($1.2M, $600,000 city mixed-use grants).
Maplewood Mall $3.3M remake breaks ground (about 50% of the mall's storefronts vacant in 2018); the Germantown Special Services District BID disbands amid mismanagement claims.

Planning Commission approves (April 16) transfer of the Town Hall to PAID for an all-commercial reuse anchored by YouthBuild, which must occupy by Q3 2028; the YWCA developer's rights lapsed end-2024 with no new RFP.

status_now.text: Germantown has had no BID since 2019; Germantown United is drafting a five-year plan to link West Chelten Ave, Maplewood Mall and Market Square (lighting, cameras, absentee landlords). Historic Germantown opened a visitor center in July 2026 (about 125,000 visits a year); Weavers Way and several cafes opened, one brewery reports its worst finances in 6.5 years, and the CDC names gentrification as a major community concern. The Town Hall transfer was approved in April 2026; the YWCA still has no developer.

districts.lesson: A plan-and-grant approach with a thin CDC and no landlord role moved vacancy 3.5 points in eleven years while two public anchor buildings sat empty. Controlling a few key buildings matters more than another plan.

waverly.vacancy_note: The Banner (Oct 2026) found more than 1 in 4 buildings in the Waverly Main Street district (29th-35th St) appear completely empty, and the city does not track long-term empty storefronts. waverly.income_note: Conflicting figures: the project brief/proposal gives tract median family income of about 36-61% of area median (poverty 12-30%), while sponsor tract data show median household incomes of $103,750 (47 rows) and $68,569 (21 rows). Check against ACS block groups before use.
waverly.historic: Waverly Main Street Historic District, National Register listed 31 Dec 2013 (ref. 13001020): about 31 acres and 141 properties along Greenmount from about 29th to 35th St; 70 of 79 frontage properties are inside it. waverly.anchor_institution: Johns Hopkins University, about a mile west (30,210 students in fall 2024; JHU offices in the former Eastern High School on 33rd St); Central Baltimore Partnership works in the area.
waverly.ownership_note: Ownership is concentrated: LLCs controlled by one owner hold 11 Greenmount properties, most with empty storefronts (The Banner, 5 Oct 2026).
waverly.city_note: Baltimore city: population 569,997 (2025 estimate), 59.2% Black, median household income $62,177 (2020-24), 19.7% in poverty. Waverly neighbourhood: 3,551 people (2010) at about 24,000 per sq mi.
waverly.zoning_note: Sponsor data flag 68 of 79 frontage properties as C-1; the study block's zoning was not independently confirmed.
waverly.urban_renewal_note: The city lists a 'Waverly Business Area' urban renewal plan (2012) with a 2011 amendment; the brief's 1979 plan and its ban on new taverns, liquor stores and pawnshops could not be verified.

aversion.research: Caoui, Hollenbeck & Osborne (2022 working paper): about one grocery lost per three dollar stores within 2 miles, and fresh-produce buying down 4-7.4% (up to 30.4% for low-income households); no study links dollar stores to crime.

aversion.waverly_evidence: In 2018 the Waverly Improvement Association fought the Waverly Tavern licence (38th St and Old York Rd, outside the study block) over drug dealing and loitering; it was suspended for a week and fined $2,500.
aversion.law: Conditional use by City Council ordinance in C-1 and at least 300 ft from other alcohol retail (Sec. 14-336); no new licence within 300 ft of a church or school (MD Alc. Bev. Sec. 12-1605); stores in residential zones phased out by 2019 (Sec. 18-701); the claimed urban renewal ban is unverified.
aversion.research: Baltimore studies: each 10% more outlet access went with 4.2% more violent crime, worse for package stores (2018); closing 80 non-conforming stores was linked to 22 fewer homicides a year (2020); liquor and corner stores have about 25% more violent crime nearby (2016).

food & drink|food & drink.basis: Restaurants cluster to share demand when distance rules are lifted and become more varied (Milan); drop to 0 for identical formats such as two carry-outs.

food & drink|retail goods.basis: Shop rental income rises with passing footfall and nearby shops (elasticity at least 0.25, Dutch streets).

food & drink|personal services.basis: Daily services and coffee or food share trips; only general footfall evidence, no pair study.

food & drink|entertainment & assembly.basis: Arts audiences spend $38.46 per event beyond admission, including dining; live music can attach to restaurants as a conditional use.

food & drink|office.basis: Daytime workers buy lunch and coffee; no pair-specific study found.

food & drink|production & light industry.basis: Light food processing is allowed in C-1; +1 if the maker has a shop front, -1 if noise, dust or smell reaches outdoor seating.

food & drink|institutional & religious.basis: Restaurant (Class B) licences are exempt from the 300-ft church and school rule; package or tavern licences within 300 ft of St. John's are -1.

food & drink|residential.basis: Restaurants are allowed even in residential zones, but outdoor dining beside homes is conditional and night noise is capped; daytime cafe +1, late-night or carry-out -1.

food & drink|vacant.basis: A dark storefront raises nearby property crime until it reopens and removes footfall (Los Angeles).

retail goods|retail goods.basis: Shops gain from each other's footfall; -1 for duplicate discount, convenience or small-box formats.

retail goods|personal services.basis: A daily-needs cluster such as a shop next to a barber; only general footfall evidence.

retail goods|entertainment & assembly.basis: Shops mostly close before evening events, so little overlap.

retail goods|production & light industry.basis: +1 if the maker sells on site.

retail goods|institutional & religious.basis: No distance rule for retail without alcohol; package liquor within 300 ft of a church or school, or a smoke shop within 750 ft of a school or park, is -1.

retail goods|residential.basis: Single-use commercial blocks had about 45% more crime than blocks with housing (Los Angeles); retail without alcohol is allowed in residential zones.

retail goods|vacant.basis: Store closures cut nearby business counts and jobs, partly through fewer shopping trips.

personal services|personal services.basis: Destination services with loyal clients; mild competition between identical formats.

personal services|institutional & religi.basis: Barbers and salons are allowed by right; body art next to a church or school is a -1 review flag.

personal services|residential.basis: Personal services are allowed in residential zones and mixed blocks are safer; amplified fitness classes before 7 am or after 9 pm are -1.

personal services|vacant.basis: Dark frontage lowers footfall and safety for neighbours.

entertainment & assembly|entertainment &.basis: The zoning board must weigh how many similar venues are nearby (saturation).

entertainment & assembly|office.basis: Offices are empty at night, so little conflict and no evidence of synergy.

entertainment & assembly|production & li.basis: Both tolerate noise and can buffer each other away from homes.

entertainment & assembly|institutional &.basis: Live-entertainment approval must weigh closeness to places of worship and schools; a quiet gallery scores 0.

entertainment & assembly|residential.basis: Noise cap of 58 dB(A), 53 after 9 pm, at the residential line; entertainment audible beyond 50 ft is banned; late venues raise assaults.

entertainment & assembly|vacant.basis: Dark frontage lowers footfall and safety on patrons' walking routes.

office|office.basis: Neutral, but long runs of frontage that is dark in the evening weaken eyes on the street.

office|residential.basis: Offices are allowed in residential zones; compatible but no synergy.

office|vacant.basis: Blight effects reach all neighbours; offices rely less on footfall, so a weaker penalty is defensible.

production & light industry|production &.basis: Shared suppliers and customers against cumulative noise.

production & light industry|institutiona.basis: Loud work during services or funerals would be -1; not legally restricted.

production & light industry|residential.basis: Enclosed small-scale making and light food processing are allowed in C-1; noisy or smelly work 9 pm-7 am next to homes is -1.

production & light industry|vacant.basis: Blight and burglary exposure; makers rely less on footfall.

institutional & religious|institutional.basis: Neutral; clusters of weekday-dark institutional frontage are a mild concern.

institutional & religious|residential.basis: Places of worship are allowed everywhere with design rules; treatment centres are not crime magnets compared with retail (Baltimore).

institutional & religious|vacant.basis: Blight lowers visitors' sense of safety.

residential|vacant.basis: Cleaning up vacant lots cut residents' safety worries 58% and gun violence 29% (Philadelphia trial); fixing abandoned buildings cut gun assaults 39%.

vacant|vacant.basis: Lost footfall and closure spillovers compound.

adjacency.notes: Scores are -1 conflict, 0 neutral, +1 complement. Where the notes gave two tags (such as R/L), 'kind' uses the first one. Apply the rules after the category score; they matter more on Greenmount than the grid. Weights are a judgement: 1.0 next door, 0.5 across the street, 0 beyond the block, but legal radii (300, 750, 2,640 ft) apply in full on either side. The matrix assumes C-1 zoning; most pair cells rest on judgement.
